- Stack: TypeScript everywhere. Phaser renders the client (`apps/web`), Colyseus runs the authoritative server (`apps/server`), and a pure fixed-step simulation (`packages/simulation`) is shared by both. The layout follows §17.
-- Build and test commands: none yet; the skeleton feature adds them here.

+- Build and test commands (from the repository root, Node 24): install `npm ci`; develop `npm run dev` (server on 2593, web on 5393); check `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:integration`; build `npm run build` (then `npm start` runs the built server); browser `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts`.
- Authoritative logic (`packages/simulation`, `packages/protocol`, `packages/content`) never imports Phaser, Colyseus, DOM APIs, wall-clock time or `Math.random`.
- Boundaries: never change `docs/spec.docx`, `docs/spec.md` or anything under `features/`.

+A browser multiplayer pirate treasure race. The game is specified in [`docs/spec.md`](docs/spec.md) (the text of `docs/spec.docx`); [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) maps this repository onto it.

+This is the walking skeleton. Browsers create or join a private match by a six-character code, sail placeholder ships with WASD or the arrow keys, and every browser in the match sees the positions the authoritative server decides.
+Node 24 and npm 11. The browser tests use Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0, which must already be installed.
+| Develop (server on 2593, web on 5393, both from source) | `npm run dev` |
+| Integration tests (a real server in-process, headless clients) | `npm run test:integration` |
+| Build every package and the web client | `npm run build` |
+| Browser tests (start the server and web client themselves) | `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts` |
+Set `VITE_SERVER_URL` when the web client should reach a server other than port 2593 on its own host.
+| `apps/web` | Phaser client: landing page, HUD, input, interpolated rendering |
+| `packages/simulation` | Pure fixed-step simulation shared by client and server |
+| `packages/protocol` | Message schemas, validation and the protocol version |
+| `packages/content` | Map, spawn slots, tuning, rules presets and frame budgets |
+| `tests/unit`, `tests/integration`, `tests/e2e` | Cross-package unit tests, server integration tests, Playwright scenarios |
+| `assets/source`, `assets/exported`, `infra` | Placeholders for art sources, runtime assets and deployment |

+The walking skeleton of the §14 browser architecture: browsers join a private match on one authoritative Colyseus room, the shared fixed-step simulation moves the ships, and every browser draws the server's result.
+| Workspace | §14 component | What it holds now |
+| `apps/web` | Browser client and web shell | Landing page (create or join by code), HUD, keyboard input adapter, input sender, snapshot interpolation, Phaser scene drawing placeholder ships |
+| `apps/server` | Match process | `MatchRoom` (one Colyseus room per match), the Schema mirror of the simulation state, per-client input gate, server bootstrap |
+| `packages/simulation` | Combat simulation (shared fixed-step functions) | Integer match state, seeded generator, 60 Hz `step` with world logic every third step, `hashState` |
+| `packages/protocol` | Data contracts (§16) | Protocol version, join options, the input message schema (zod) and its validation, refusal codes and messages |
+| `packages/content` | Content and tuning (§17) | Sea map, spawn slots, ship speed, private-match rules, the `slice` and `alpha` rules presets and §8's frame budgets, with validators |
+| `packages/test-tools` | Test harness (§17) | `HeadlessClient`: a browserless player on the real Colyseus SDK |
+The HTTP service, PostgreSQL, static hosting and monitoring are not built yet (`infra/` is a placeholder).

+- **Purity.** `simulation`, `protocol` and `content` import no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`; their tsconfig leaves out the DOM library, and `tests/unit/purity.test.ts` fails on a violation.

+- **Integers.** Every number in the simulation state is an integer. Positions are sub-units (256 per 16 px tile) on a 48 × 32 tile sea with the origin top-left. Diagonals are normalised with an integer square root, so `hashState` (64-bit FNV-1a over a canonical serialization) does not depend on the JavaScript engine.

+- **One clock.** The room steps the simulation 60 times a second with Colyseus `setFixedTimestep`, the accumulator-based successor of `setSimulationInterval`. World logic runs on frames divisible by 3 (20 Hz); the room then mirrors the plain state into its Colyseus Schema, which Colyseus patches to clients at 20 Hz.

+- **The server alone writes state.** Clients send only `input` messages: `{seq, frame, buttons, moveX, moveY}`. `InputGate` drops, and counts, messages over the rate cap (60 per second of match time) or over 128 bytes, malformed ones (including axes outside [-1, 1], which are rejected rather than clamped), ones with a sequence number that is not higher than the last one, and ones tagged more than 30 frames ahead of the server. A held input lapses to neutral after 15 frames without a fresh one. Unknown message types are dropped. Colyseus's own limits sit above these and do disconnect: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB and more than 240 messages a second.

+- **Joining.** `create` makes a room whose code is generated on the server. `join` finds a room by code through `filterBy(['code'])`. The room's static `onAuth` refuses a mismatched protocol version (426), an unknown code (404) or a full match (409, eight players) with a readable message that the client shows.

+- **Rendering.** The client keeps a snapshot buffer per ship and draws 100 ms in the past, interpolating between patches. The HUD lists the latest decoded server positions without interpolation. Prediction and reconciliation are left to the combat spike.

+npm workspaces, TypeScript 7.0.2 (`tsc` for typechecks and package builds), Vite 8.3.0 (web build), Vitest 5.0.1 (`unit` and `integration` projects), Phaser 4.2.1, `colyseus` 0.18.8 with `@colyseus/schema` 5.0.34, `@colyseus/sdk` 0.18.4, zod 4.6.5, Playwright 1.63.0. Every one is the current major; none is pinned to a previous one. Workspace packages export a `@pirate-sea-race/source` condition that points at `src/`. Vite, Vitest, tsx and `tsc` typechecks resolve through it, so development and tests need no build. `npm run build` compiles each package to `dist/` in dependency order, and `node apps/server/dist/main.js` runs the built server. `colyseus` brings `uWebSockets.js` in from GitHub as a peer dependency, so `npm ci` needs access to github.com as well as the npm registry.

# Decisions: skeleton-fixes

From the operator session of 2026-09-24, after the independent review of run skeleton-001 blocked its candidate (general and coverage reviewers, one P1 each).

## Decisions

- This is a follow-up feature on top of skeleton-001's candidate (snapshot `50b14b3`, branch `skeleton/candidate-001`), not a new run of `skeleton`: the lane starts from the reviewed code and changes only what `game-task.md` lists. Reviewers review this diff; the skeleton's own requirements in `features/skeleton/` still apply.
- Scope is findings 1–11 of `game-task.md`: both P1s, the P2s that are cheap to close (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) and three findings from the operator's code review (9, 10, 11). The general reviewer's P2 about `allocateCode` exhausting its 16 attempts is deferred.
- Private-match admission: the client's `create` request carries a one-time random `createToken` (at least 128 bits, generated with the platform's crypto API outside the pure packages). The room keeps it privately (never in its state, listing or metadata) and admits exactly one seat carrying it: the creator's. Every other seat must carry `code` equal to the room's code, whatever matchmaker method reserved it. The room enforces this itself in its instance-level `onAuth` or `onJoin` by throwing a `ServerError` with a readable message. The worker may choose an equivalent mechanism only if it also closes the window between the room's listing and the creator's seat.
- The join options change, so `PROTOCOL_VERSION` goes from 1 to 2; tests and the HUD read the constant, not a literal.
- The build output is proven inside the existing `build` check: `npm run build` finishes with a smoke script under `scripts/` that runs the built server on a free port, creates a match through `@colyseus/sdk` and stops it. The policy stays unchanged, and `build` runs before `browser` in the verifier's order.
- The generic matchmaker failure (`MATCHMAKE_INVALID_CRITERIA`) is shown as "That match is full or no longer exists"; "No match with that code" is kept for the server's own 404 refusal.

## Assumptions

- Colyseus 0.18's instance `onAuth(client, options)` or `onJoin(client, options)` can refuse a seat by throwing, and the client receives the error's message.
- Frame tags keep their current meaning in this feature: checked against the 30-frame future window, then applied from the next step. Only the documentation changes.
- `tests/reporters/testSummary.ts` stays registered in `vitest.config.ts`; new test files need nothing extra to be counted.
- The lane may add test files anywhere under its owned paths and may adjust existing tests only where a finding says they are wrong (finding 10, and literals of the protocol version).

## Deferred

- `allocateCode` failing after 16 attempts (reachable only with extreme numbers of live rooms).
- Frame-accurate input application, client prediction and reconciliation: the combat spike.
- Replacing the `colyseus` meta-package with `@colyseus/core`, `@colyseus/ws-transport` and `@colyseus/schema` (it would drop `uWebSockets.js` fetched from GitHub during `npm ci`).
- Matchmaking with a driver other than the local one (Redis), whose metadata filtering must be rechecked.
- Vitest support in md-manager's verifier (`text_test_counts` in `workflow/checks.py`); it belongs to md-manager, not this repository.

Design challenge attempt 1 paused the run before any worker launch. Concerns:
  P1 [failure_mode] The plan checks the code in the room itself (instance onAuth/onJoin). Colyseus runs those only after its HTTP matchmaker has already reserved a seat and sent the reservation back to the caller. A `join` or `joinOrCreate` without a code gets no `filterBy` filter, and a `joinById` to any known roomId is also allowed. All of these still receive a reservation for some private match. In Colyseus, that reservation carries the room's listing, and the listing (RoomCache.toJSON) includes `metadata`. `MatchRoom.onCreate` puts `{ code }` into that metadata (apps/server/src/MatchRoom.ts:86). So a caller without the code can read the code from the reservation's JSON, get refused when the WebSocket connects, then join again with the code. Each unused reservation also counts toward `maxClients` until `seatReservationTime` runs out. # Task: game

## Goal

Fix what the independent review of run skeleton-001 found in the walking skeleton on this branch: private matches must be unjoinable without their code, a check must prove the server runs from its build output, and the review's test gaps must be closed. Everything else about the skeleton stays as it is.

## Context

- This branch starts from skeleton-001's reviewed candidate (the `skeleton` feature: `features/skeleton/game-task.md` and `features/skeleton/decisions.md` still describe what the skeleton must do, and all of it still applies). Read `docs/architecture.md` first, then the files named below.
- The verifier runs `npm ci` in a clean worktree, then `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:integration`, `npm run build` and `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts`. Each must pass from a clean checkout.
- The verifier reads unit and integration test counts only from a Node test-runner summary (`# tests N`, `# pass N`, `# fail N`, `# skipped N`). `tests/reporters/testSummary.ts`, registered in `vitest.config.ts`, prints Vitest's counts in that form. Keep it registered; without it every passing test run is refused as "no passing test evidence".
- Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0 is installed and shared read-only; never run `playwright install`.

Review findings to fix (reviewer, severity):

1. (general, P1) `authorizeEntry` in `apps/server/src/MatchRoom.ts` treats any request without `code` as a create. Colyseus 0.18 exposes `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` over its HTTP matchmaker too. A `join` with only `{protocolVersion}` gets no `filterBy` filter, so it seats the caller in an arbitrary open private match, and the room never checks the code itself.
2. (coverage, P1) No check starts the server from its build output. `npm run build` only compiles; the integration tests and the Playwright web server run the TypeScript sources through the `@pirate-sea-race/source` condition. A broken `dist/` (including the workspace packages' `default` → `./dist/*.js` exports) passes all five checks.
3. (general, P2) Two joins racing for the eighth seat: the loser gets Colyseus's `MATCHMAKE_INVALID_CRITERIA`, which `refusalMessage` in `apps/web/src/connection.ts` shows as "No match with that code" although the match exists.
4. (general, P2) `InputGate` uses an input's frame tag only for the future-window check; accepted input applies from the next step whatever frame it names. Acceptable without prediction, but undocumented.
5. (coverage, P2) Only the headless SDK path checks refusal messages; `refusalMessage` and its display in `#join-error` have no test for the protocol-mismatch and full-match refusals.
6. (coverage, P2) Nothing tests the room's clock: a misread `setFixedTimestep` argument or `patchRate` would pass every test.
7. (coverage, P2) Interpolation is tested only inside `SnapshotBuffer`; nothing proves the client draws interpolated rather than latest positions.
8. (coverage, P2) The decision that the step function uses no floating-point transcendental functions is not enforced by any test.

Found by the operator's code review of the same candidate:

9. `mapBounds` in `packages/simulation/src/config.ts` makes positions inclusive up to `widthTiles * subUnitsPerTile`, so a ship clamped to the edge sits in tile `widthTiles`, one tile outside the map.
10. The integration test "lets two clients join the same code and see the same authoritative movement" always holds `moveX: 1` for 600 ms; from the rightmost spawn slot that leaves a margin of about one world step before the edge clamps it. Move toward the map centre, as the e2e test does.
11. `headingOf` in `packages/simulation/src/step.ts` builds its lookup object on every call; `apps/web/src/seaScene.ts` formats the slot colour by hand instead of using `cssColor` from `matchView.ts`.

## Constraints

- Change only what these findings need; keep the file layout, naming and patterns of the existing code (tagged results at trust boundaries, zod schemas as the source of types, injected dependencies, doc comments citing spec sections).
- The pure packages stay pure (`CLAUDE.md`). Keep every existing test passing; change a test only where a finding says it is wrong.
- Keep the policy's check commands and the two browser scenario ids unchanged. Never change `docs/spec.docx`, `docs/spec.md` or `features/`.
- No new runtime dependency unless an existing one cannot do the job; if you add one, pin it exactly and say why in `docs/architecture.md`.

## Acceptance

- Finding 1: every seat except the creator's must present the room's code, enforced by the room itself, not only by matchmaking filters (see `decisions.md`). Integration tests show that `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` without a code or with a wrong code are refused with a readable message, that the creator still gets in, and that the room keeps running for its players.
- Finding 2: `npm run build` ends by starting the built server (`node apps/server/dist/main.js` on a free port), waiting for `/__healthcheck`, creating a private match through `@colyseus/sdk` against it and seeing the creator's ship, then stopping the server; a failure fails the build. The script lives under `scripts/`.
- Finding 3: a join that fails with the generic matchmaker error shows a message that does not claim the match is missing (for example "That match is full or no longer exists"); the server's own 404/409/426 refusals keep their exact messages.
- Finding 4: `docs/architecture.md` states the frame-tag limitation in one or two sentences, and when the combat spike must change it.
- Finding 5: unit tests cover `refusalMessage` for the protocol-mismatch, unknown-code, full-match and generic-matchmaker cases and an unreachable server.
- Finding 6: an integration test shows the room advances about 60 frames per second (tolerance at least ±15 %) and sends state patches no faster than 20 Hz plus tolerance.
- Finding 7: a unit test shows `MatchView.renderPosition` returns a position between two snapshots 100 ms behind `now`, not the latest snapshot.
- Finding 8: the purity test also rejects `Math.sqrt`, `Math.cbrt`, `Math.hypot`, `Math.pow`, `Math.exp`, `Math.log*` and the trigonometric `Math` functions in the pure packages, with a sample in its self-test.
- Findings 9–11: fixed, with a unit test for the map edge (a ship clamped to the edge lies on the last tile).
- `npm ci` then each of the five policy checks passes from a clean checkout.

Browser checks: each scenario id appears in exactly one test title as `[scenario:<id>]`. That test, when it passes, attaches exactly one image/png named `screenshot:<id>` (other attachments are fine). The verifier refuses anything else. ## Stop

Report `blocked` instead of continuing when any of these happens:

- `npm ci` or an install fails twice for reasons outside the repository (registry, network).

- After ninety minutes of work, any required check still fails and you cannot name the next fix.

- Scope is findings 1–11 of `game-task.md`: both P1s, the P2s that are cheap to close (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) and the operator's code-review findings 10 and 11. Finding 9 is already fixed in this base. The general reviewer's P2 about `allocateCode` exhausting its 16 attempts is deferred.

  - (b) The room is registered with `filterBy(["code", "createToken"])`. A `create` carries a one-time random `createToken` of at least 128 bits, generated with the platform's crypto API outside the pure packages. Colyseus copies `filterBy` fields from the create options into the listing's metadata, so `onCreate` must replace the metadata (`setMatchmaking`) so it never keeps the token. A request carrying a token then matches no existing listing: `join` fails, and `joinOrCreate` can only create.
  - (c) The room's `onJoin` (or instance `onAuth`) is the backstop, which also covers `joinById`. It admits exactly one seat carrying the token stored in `onCreate` (the creator's); every other seat must carry `code` equal to `this.state.code`.
  - What remains: someone who already knows a roomId (a current or former member) can reserve seats through `joinById` until they expire. `docs/architecture.md` records this.

# Decisions: skeleton-fixes

From the operator session of 2026-09-24, after the independent review of run skeleton-001 blocked its candidate (general and coverage reviewers, one P1 each).

## Decisions

Every other seat must carry `code` equal to the room's code, whatever matchmaker method reserved it. The worker may choose an equivalent mechanism only if it also closes the window between the room's listing and the creator's seat.

I've fixed the plan, and it was small. I left the edits uncommitted on purpose: `resume` commits them on the run's branch itself, then runs the challenge again.

**What I verified in Colyseus 0.18.16 before editing:**
- **Seat squatting, from the challenge's P1, is real.** A code-less HTTP `join` reserves a seat in an arbitrary private match before any room-level check runs, so my room-only plan wouldn't have stopped it.
- **The code-leak half is wrong for this version.** `buildSeatReservation` returns only `name`, `sessionId`, `roomId` and `processId`, with no listing metadata. I recorded this as an assumption so the worker doesn't chase it.
- **Finding 9 is already fixed.** The worker corrected `mapBounds` after my tick-3 review, and a test covers it. I missed that in later ticks.

**What changed in `features/skeleton-fixes/`:**
- **`decisions.md`:** match admission now has the challenge's three layers:
  - The static `onAuth` refuses requests that carry neither a code nor a `createToken`, or carry both, before a seat is reserved. The existing 404/409/426 refusals stay there.
  - `filterBy(["code", "createToken"])`, with `onCreate` replacing the metadata. Colyseus copies filter fields from the create options into the listing metadata, which the challenge didn't mention, so without this the token would stay in the listing.
  - The room's `onJoin` as the backstop, which also covers `joinById`.

  The leftover gap is recorded: someone who already knows a roomId can still reserve seats through `joinById`. I also added the challenge's P2s: refusal messages under 100 bytes, and a smoke script that uses `PORT=0`, limits every wait and always kills the server.
- **`game-task.md`:** finding 1's acceptance now includes these tests:
  - code-less requests reserve no seat;
  - a `joinOrCreate` carrying a token always creates a new match;
  - the listing never contains the token.

  Finding 2's acceptance now spells out the smoke script's rules. Finding 9 says "change nothing".

content.text: The challenge passed on attempt 2 (8 P2 concerns, nothing blocking), and the `game` worker has been running since 09:52. I'll set up a watch on the run's timeline so every new event wakes me:

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on

Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. content.content:
- P2 assumption | Layer (b) says onCreate must 'replace the metadata (setMatchmaking)'. In Colyseus 0.16/0.17, setMatchmaking({metadata}) goes through setMetadata, which merges field by field into the existing listing.metadata. It does not replace it. If 0.18 behaves the same way, `setMatchmaking({ metadata: { code, custom } })` (MatchRoom.ts:86, unchanged) keeps a createToken that filterBy copied from the create options.
- P2 failure_mode | The acceptance test 'a joinOrCreate carrying a token creates a new match and never lands in an existing one' is only meaningful if it reuses the creator's own token from an existing match. With a fresh token, no listing can match whether or not the metadata was scrubbed, so the test passes even when layer (b) is broken.
- P2 other | 'join, joinOrCreate and joinById without a code … are refused with the exact short message' only makes sense for requests carrying neither a code nor a token. Static onAuth cannot tell the methods apart. So `join {createToken}` passes layer (a) and fails with Colyseus's generic MATCHMAKE_INVALID_CRITERIA text, and `joinOrCreate {createToken}` is meant to create.
- P2 assumption | The browser has to generate the createToken. `crypto.randomUUID()` gives only 122 random bits, below the required 128, and exists only in secure contexts. `serverEndpoint` uses location.hostname, so the client is meant to work on plain-http LAN hosts too.
- P2 failure_mode | Room-level refusals and joinById outcomes are new SDK error shapes: a room error after the WebSocket opens, and MATCHMAKE_INVALID_ROOM_ID. Finding 5's unit tests for refusalMessage will probably hand-build error objects. The unreachable-server branch depends on `error instanceof TypeError`, which holds only if @colyseus/sdk 0.18.4 does not wrap fetch failures.
- P2 failure_mode | The smoke script's child server outlives the script unless it is killed explicitly. On Linux a spawned child is not killed when its parent exits or throws. SIGTERM goes through Colyseus gracefullyShutdown, which can wait on rooms to dispose. @colyseus/sdk is not a root dependency; it resolves from scripts/ only because npm hoists it from apps/web and test-tools.
- P2 other | Refusal messages are required to stay under 100 bytes, but protocolMismatchMessage embeds the client-supplied version. For a request with no protocolVersion it produces '…speaks vundefined…', which is 106 bytes. Under layer (a), a malformed code without a token becomes 400 instead of today's 404 'No match with that code', so a player who types a short code gets the malformed-request text.
- P2 assumption | Finding 6's clock test may show that the base is wrong. It is unclear whether `setFixedTimestep(cb, STEPS_PER_SECOND)` takes a rate or a step length in ms. If it takes ms, the room runs at about 16.7 steps per second and every existing test still passes.

Your `scp` went through an SSH config alias, `vea-vps`. That alias carries the right user and key for this server, and the raw `agentops@159.65.150.122` I gave you doesn't, so the server refused it. Use the alias for the tunnel too:

```bash
ssh -N -L '5393:[::1]:5393' -L 2593:127.0.0.1:2593 vea-vps
```

- **Quoted `[::1]`:** if your laptop uses zsh, unquoted brackets are treated as a glob and fail with "no matches found".
- **Silence means it works:** with `-N` the command just sits there with no prompt. Leave it running, then open `http://localhost:5393` on your laptop in two windows.
- **Any login user works:** whichever user `vea-vps` logs in as is fine, because the tunnel only forwards to this machine's loopback ports, where the servers are listening.

The "Permanently added '159.65.150.122'" line just saved this server's host key on your laptop. It's harmless and needs no action.

If the tunnel connects but the page doesn't load, run `ssh -v -N -L …` and paste the lines that mention `channel` or `forwarding`.

That error means the terminal you ran it in doesn't know the name `vea-vps`. This VPS (hostname `agents`) has no such alias; it only exists on the machine where your `scp` worked. So you most likely ran the tunnel in a pane that's logged into the VPS, not on your laptop.

1. **Open a local terminal on your laptop**, the same kind of window where you ran `scp ~/Downloads/... vea-vps:...`, not a Herdr or SSH session on the server.
2. Run the tunnel there:
   ```bash
   ssh -N -L '5393:[::1]:5393' -L 2593:127.0.0.1:2593 vea-vps
   ```
3. Leave it running. With `-N` it shows no prompt. Then open `http://localhost:5393` in your laptop's browser.

If you're sure you're on the laptop and it still can't resolve `vea-vps`, the alias is set somewhere unexpected. Run this on the laptop and paste the output:

```bash
ssh -G vea-vps | grep -E '^(hostname|user|identityfile) '
```

content.content:
## 1 The player experience

### Core loop

Spawn at a fair starting location, sail toward a lead, explore an island, gain a power or rubbing, assess nearby rivals, fight or evade, and choose the next destination. Once all four types are held, the compass reveals the final treasure. The player must still travel there and defend the claim.

Three decisions should repeatedly matter: where to go next, whether a fight is worth the lost time, and which abilities suit the player’s approach. Sailing should create encounters and anticipation; it must not become several minutes of empty travel.

### A representative match

A player starts beside a small ship, finds a Smoke fruit on a nearby island, and reads a rumor pointing to a western ruin. Another player reaches that ruin first and leaves with the Moon rubbing. The first player can chase them or investigate a second lead.

Later, the Smoke player wins a boarding duel and steals the Moon rubbing. The defeated opponent keeps their other two rubbings and Ember powers. They respawn away from the winner and pursue a different Moon source. A third player completes all four types, triggering a public rumor about the final island’s sector. The remaining players must decide whether to finish their own collection or intercept the leader.

### Design commitments

- Exploration and fighting are both viable ways to advance. A player can win without initiating PvP, but cannot assume they will avoid it.
- Fruit powers change play style. Finding the rarest-looking power must not automatically decide the match.
- PvP produces a meaningful setback without erasing the loser’s whole match.
- The destination is earned through information and inventory. Defeating the most opponents is not a substitute victory condition.
- Every important attack has readable startup and a defensive answer available to every kit.
- The first prototype must prove the online duel and the theft loop before adding a large content roster.

### Scope boundary

The first release is a repeatable session game. Persistent shared worlds, crews, ranked seasons, elaborate naval combat, trading, sprawling quests, and mobile touch combat are later possibilities. Each would materially change balancing or production requirements.

## 3 The sea and islands

Use a top-down tile world with a fixed navigable layout and authored island templates. Randomize their contents and approved placements. Avoid unrestricted procedural geography in the first release: travel fairness and recognizable landmarks are more valuable than unlimited map variation.

| Element | Initial content and behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Sea | Connected routes, shoals as obstacles, clear docking areas |
| Islands | 12 islands drawn from tropical, volcanic, ruin, and mist themes |
| Final island | One of several validated hidden sockets; reachable by every ship |
| Ruins | One globally claimable rubbing source on each regular island |
| Other loot | Fruit pedestals, supply chests, rumor signs, and gold caches |
| Landmarks | Visible silhouettes that help players navigate without opening a map |
| Hazards | Clearly marked slow zones; no lethal environmental traps in version one |

### Movement and visibility

Sailing uses acceleration, braking, and turning, with generous handling rather than a naval simulation. Nearby ships and islands are visible inside a defined sight radius. Unvisited territory is covered by fog on the minimap. Once discovered, terrain stays on the personal map, while enemies disappear outside current visibility.

World positions are authoritative on the server. Island discovery, enemy visibility, and rumors are evaluated there. The client receives only the hidden-state information it is entitled to know. Public terrain can be shared; objective locations and the final-island choice must not be recoverable from a public random seed.

### Exploration activities

Each ruin uses one of two short interactions: a three-symbol sequence or a small navigation puzzle. Reading nearby clues solves it; no external One Piece knowledge is required. Completing it permits a six-second rubbing interaction that can be interrupted by a valid encounter. Total time at a fresh ruin should be about 20–40 seconds.

Rumors identify an island or sector containing a type the player lacks. Stale rumors are visibly marked after their target is claimed. The journal offers a replacement lead from remaining sources or a coarse carrier sighting. It never guarantees that the destination will remain uncontested.

Target neighboring-island travel at 20–40 seconds and the longest useful crossing at 90 seconds or less. Tune map size around those times. Remove empty stretches before adding more sailing mechanics.

## 4 Poneglyph ownership and theft

Poneglyphs are stationary ancient inscriptions. Players carry their physical rubbings. Use four distinct symbols: Sun, Moon, Tide, and Storm. The match contains three individually identified rubbings of each type, for 12 total. Each of the 12 regular islands begins with one sealed source; assignment is server-controlled.

| Rule | Exact behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Collection | Hold interact for six uninterrupted seconds at an unlocked source |
| Inventory | At most one rubbing of each type per player |
| Duplicates | Cannot collect or steal a type already held; it stays with its owner |
| Completion | Holding all four types enables final navigation and claiming |
| Normal defeat | Winner chooses one loser-held type that the winner lacks |
| Theft deadline | Five-second choice; default to the eligible type with fewest free sources, then fixed type order |
| No eligible type | No rubbing transfers; the gold reward still applies |
| Draw | Neither player loses rubbings or gold |
| Dropping or trading | Players cannot voluntarily drop, trade, copy, or destroy rubbings |

Each rubbing has exactly one location: sealed at a source, owned by a player, held in a recovery cache, or reserved inside an unresolved duel transaction. Its unique ID persists through every transfer. There is no new rubbing spawn when a player loses.

### Why multiple copies and limited theft

A single global copy of each type would let one player or an abandoned session block the whole match. Three copies allow competing routes to victory. Limiting theft to one type preserves tension without turning a single mistake into a full reset. Players cannot hoard duplicates to remove every route for everyone else.

This is a proposed tradeoff: the match has less total-loot brutality than an elimination game, but more opportunities for recovery and rivalry. Measure whether exploration alone is too fast before reducing the supply.

### Transfer invariants

Commit a duel result and its inventory changes together, once, on the authoritative match process. A repeated result message must not repeat a transfer. Validate winner eligibility again at commit time. The 12 rubbing IDs must remain accounted for until the match ends, including when a player quits during resolution.

## 5 Finding and claiming the final treasure

When a player first holds all four types, their compass reveals the final island’s exact route. The match announces that a complete set exists and reveals the island’s broad sea sector to everyone. All ships may travel there; four rubbings are required to claim the treasure, not to physically enter the island.

This creates a final interception opportunity without requiring every challenger to have completed their own collection. A challenger with fewer than four can stop a leader through a duel, but cannot win until they complete their own set.

### Claim sequence

1. Reach the treasure circle while holding all four rubbing types.
1. End any protection state, stop moving, and hold interact for ten seconds.
1. Remain connected, eligible, and free of an accepted duel reservation for the entire channel.
1. On completion, the server commits the winner and freezes all match outcomes.

Only one claim channel can be active at a time. A second eligible player must interrupt through a valid challenge or wait. Characters do not body-block one another in the overworld. Moving, losing eligibility, disconnecting, or entering a duel resets claim progress to zero.

### Counterplay and information

Anyone in engagement range can interrupt a claim by successfully starting a duel. The claim UI shows this risk explicitly. Duels remain 1v1: surrounding players cannot damage the fighters or join halfway through. After a duel, the winner receives eight seconds to move away; objective interactions end that protection.

Losing a rubbing removes claim eligibility immediately. The game cannot make a person forget a destination they have already learned; the server simply refuses an ineligible claim. Final navigation becomes inactive until the set is restored.

### Resolving simultaneous actions

On each world tick, process accepted encounter reservations before advancing claim channels. If several attackers qualify in the same tick, choose the closest, then the lowest stable player ID. If several players begin claiming on the same tick, use the same distance-and-ID rule. Inputs arriving after a resolved win cannot retroactively cancel it.

The ten-second channel is a deliberate addition to the original “arrive and win” idea. Test both versions. Keep the channel only if it creates exciting finishes without repeated, frustrating stalls.

## 6 Starting and leaving encounters

Exploration and combat use different views, but remain parts of one live match. Each player can belong to at most one duel. Their overworld avatar becomes a non-interactive encounter marker while the duel runs, and their ship is reserved. Other players continue exploring.

### On islands

A player presses the challenge action within close range and line of sight. A visible 0.6-second lunge telegraphs the attempt. The defender can move or dash out of its hit area. If it connects, the server reserves both players and starts the duel. Missing incurs a six-second challenge cooldown.

### At sea

Ships use a short-range grappling action with a one-second windup and a visible aim direction. A successful grapple reserves both ships and loads the shared ship-deck arena. Escape is possible before the grapple lands. There are no cannons, sinking ships, crew stations, or separate ship health in version one.

### Reservation and transition

Eligibility requires both players to be active, close enough, unprotected, and outside another duel. A reservation atomically locks their inventories. Use a three-second transition with a visible countdown; all battle assets should already be loaded. If one client fails to become ready within ten seconds, resolve that client as forfeiting. If both fail because the server is unhealthy, cancel the encounter without rewards.

The dueling players enter with full duel health, fresh stamina, and the same starting Haki meter. World pursuit positioning does not grant a free opening hit. World boosts are suspended in duels and cannot expire into different combat statistics midway through a fight.

### Return to the world

The winner returns to the encounter location with eight seconds of escape protection. The loser respawns after 15 seconds at a validated dock away from nearby opponents, with 20 seconds of protection. A draw returns both to separate nearby points with eight seconds of protection. Objective collection, claiming, or initiating an attack ends return protection first and is then processed normally.

Keep a visible duel marker and elapsed time in the world. Live spectating is deferred to reduce stream-sniping information and avoid extra networking scope in the first build.

## 7 Fighting system

The target is the satisfaction of spacing, blocking, punishing, and reading an opponent, using a single-plane 2D arena. Start with compact move lists and short combinations. A large move catalogue and complex aerial juggling would multiply animation and balance work before the core is proven.

| System | Starting rule |
| --- | --- |
| Round | One round; 60-second clock; 1,000 health each |
| Timeout | Higher remaining health wins |
| Equal health | Ten-second overtime; then compare health again; exact tie is a draw |
| Movement | Walk, crouch, jump, forward dash, backdash; auto-face opponent |
| Attacks | Light, heavy, low, launcher, anti-air, throw, two kit specials |
| Defense | Hold back to guard; down-back guards low; universal throw escape |
| Stamina | 100 maximum; powers movement and guard integrity |
| Haki meter | 100 maximum; starts at 25; powers armor, parry, and finisher |
| Combos | Initial cap of five damaging hits before forced recovery |

Standing guard blocks high and mid attacks. Crouching guard blocks lows, avoids highs, and loses to mids. Throws beat passive guard and have a ten-frame escape window. A universal anti-air discourages repeated jumping. Guarding costs stamina; a broken guard causes a short punishable stagger, never a full-health guaranteed combo.

### Damage and recovery

Use 45 damage for a basic jab and roughly 100–150 for a committed heavy or special before scaling. Apply successive combo scaling of 100, 80, 65, 50, and 40 percent. Target ordinary successful combinations at 15–25 percent of health. The fifth damaging hit forces a non-juggleable recovery state; implement the cap in the simulation, not only in animations.

Dashes cost 20 stamina; blocking a light costs 10, a heavy 25, and a special 20. Regenerate 20 per second after one second without spending or blocking. Guard break causes 30 frames of stagger and restores 30 stamina. No healing works inside a duel. Every kit must answer throws, armor, projectiles, and evasion.

Both simultaneous lethal hits produce a draw. A KO on the final round tick takes priority over timeout comparison. The server evaluates both players’ hit events for the tick before declaring a KO, so processing order cannot invent a winner.

content.content:
## 9 Devil fruit inspired power kits

Players begin fruitless with a complete Duelist kit. Eating a fruit replaces the two kit specials. Core normals, throw, guard, and universal Haki remain. All six fruit types below are first-release candidates; the first playable slice uses Ember and Smoke only.

| Kit | Two signature specials | Advantage | Vulnerability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Duelist | Advancing thrust and counter slash | Reliable close combat and meter use | Limited long-range pressure |
| Ember | Flame bolt and rising flare | Controls space and punishes jumps | Long recovery if attacks miss |
| Smoke | Short feint dash and smoke screen | Changes spacing and obscures intent | Low direct damage; readable reappearance |
| Spring | Charged lunge and rebound kick | Fast approach with varied timing | Charge can be interrupted |
| Stone | Armored shoulder and ground burst | Wins selected close-range trades | Slow recovery; vulnerable to throws |
| Gale | Gust projectile and retreating slash | Pushes opponents and resets distance | Weak when trapped close |
| Beast | Pounce and claw sequence | Sustained close-range pressure | Telegraphs approach; limited reach |

### Acquisition and commitment

Place 12 fruit pedestals, two of each type, across fair loot routes. They are distinct from rubbing sources. Eating takes three seconds and can be interrupted. A player may inspect the kit description before committing. After a fruit is eaten, it stays for that match; there is no fruit swapping or random reroll economy in version one.

Fruit users remain viable after defeat because their fruit is retained. Fruitless Duelist remains a deliberate fighting option. Its specials must be tested against every fruit; it is not a weak starting class to escape as soon as possible.

### Constraints on powers

No permanent intangibility, unlimited flight, unavoidable screen-wide damage, automatic stun loops, or uncounterable invisibility. Smoke effects cannot hide the opponent’s health bar or remove all visual tells. Armor absorbs one eligible hit rather than making the whole move invulnerable; throws and specified armor-break attacks still work.

For the first release, fruit abilities are combat-only. This avoids a mobility fruit also becoming the best exploration and escape choice. Ships and docks handle travel; swimming and drowning are outside the initial rules. Later exploration abilities should open optional shortcuts while leaving the four objective types reachable by every kit.

## 10 Haki and match progression

Haki is the common tactical layer that lets every player answer powerful fruit abilities. It is available from the beginning; finding a rare fruit must not be the only path to competent combat.

| Ability | Initial cost | Effect and counterplay |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Armament | 30 Haki | Empower the next heavy within three seconds; breaks one-hit armor; blockable |
| Observation | 40 Haki | Six-frame parry window against strikes; loses to throws; 24-frame recovery on miss |
| Resolve finisher | 100 Haki | Large telegraphed attack; can be guarded or evaded; scales in combos |

Suggested inputs are Haki plus heavy, Haki plus dash, and Haki plus both specials. A missed parry still spends meter. There is no passive aura that negates all fruit skills, no hidden random critical hit, and no always-on damage increase from account level.

### Meter economy

Each duel starts at 25 Haki. A confirmed hit grants five meter to its attacker and three to its defender; a successful parry grants ten. Whiffing and standing still grant none. A damage instance awards meter once, including repeated projectile contacts. Cap gain at 20 per combo for either player. Unspent meter does not carry between duels.

### Limited match progression

Players can find training scrolls through island exploration or buy them with match gold. One scroll selects a Haki focus: Armament costs five less, Observation costs five less, or successful guards generate a small extra amount of meter. Only one focus can be equipped; changing it requires a dock interaction. No focus changes the player’s maximum health or base damage.

Training-scroll availability is tied to exploration and limited shop stock per player, not repeated kills. The first slice omits focuses entirely until base combat is balanced. The full eight-player alpha introduces the three choices if they create meaningful preferences.

### Account progression

Persistent rewards unlock visual customization, titles, emotes, and journal milestones. They do not grant starting rubbings, extra health, stronger fruits, better ships, or exclusive competitive moves. Saved controls, accessibility settings, and practice progress carry between sessions. Match gold, items, and powers reset every match.

## 11 Economy and comeback rules

Keep the match economy small. Its job is to create route choices and help players recover information, without overwhelming the central rubbing race.

| Source or purchase | Starting value | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting purse | 50 gold | Same for every player |
| Supply cache | 25 gold | One global claim per cache |
| Fresh ruin completion | 40 gold | Once per player per ruin; cannot farm the interaction |
| PvP victory | 20 percent of loser gold, capped at 50 | Transfer existing gold; never mint a kill reward |
| Targeted rumor | 25 gold | Lead to a missing rubbing type |
| Haki focus scroll | 75 gold | Full alpha only; one focus equipped |
| Sail tonic | 30 gold | Plus 10 percent sailing speed for 12 seconds |

Gold transfer rounds down and cannot make a balance negative. Shops are dockside objects, not permanent safe zones. Buying is a brief interaction that can be interrupted. Purchases have an idempotent request ID so retries cannot double-spend.

content.text:
Here's how I'd cut the next stages. The spec is explicit about order: *"The first prototype must prove the online duel and the theft loop before adding a large content roster"* (§1), and expanding fruits before the combat spike passes is *"the most avoidable scope risk"* (§18). So combat comes first, world systems run alongside it where their paths don't collide, and content comes last.

**Where we are:** the skeleton gives us the monorepo, the 60 Hz integer simulation, one Colyseus room, protocol validation, the headless client, the e2e harness and the build smoke test. It's approved but not on `main` yet.

## Proposed slices

| # | Feature | Spec | Delivers | Exit, provable by checks | Lanes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `duel-core` | §7, §8, §15 | A pure 1v1 duel simulation (details below) | Scenario tests: a −12 heavy is punishable, throw escape works only inside its window, simultaneous lethal hits draw, guard break staggers 30 frames. Hash-identical replays over 3,600 steps and after restore. | 1: `duel-sim` (`packages/simulation/src/duel`, `packages/content/src/moves`, `packages/test-tools/src/replay`) |
| 2 | `world-sea`, in parallel with 1 | §3, §16 | Sailing with acceleration, braking and turning; a tile map with shoals and docks as content data; sight radius; per-player Colyseus StateView; minimap fog | An integration test reads the actual network messages and shows an out-of-sight ship's position never reaches a client. e2e: sail around a shoal and dock. | 2: `world-server` (simulation, server, protocol) and `world-web` (scene, minimap, e2e) |
| 3 | `duel-online`, after 1 | §15, §19 | **The combat spike's exit:** two browsers in a duel (details below) | Automated: determinism and correction counts at 30/80/150 ms, jitter and loss. **Plus a manual playtest gate**, since "credible online" isn't something a check can prove. | 3: `duel-server`, `duel-netcode` (predictor, impairment harness), `duel-arena` (Phaser scene, controls, duel HUD, e2e) |
| 4 | `encounters-theft`, after 2 and 3 | §4, §6, part of §12 | Island challenge and sea grapple, reservation with a 3 s transition, the duel as an object inside the match room (§14), a 5 s theft choice, rubbing-ID transfer invariants, respawn and protection, disconnect during a duel | Invariant tests: every rubbing ID has exactly one owner through theft, quit and simultaneous duels | 2–3 |
| 5 | `objectives-endgame` | §2, §4, §5, §11, §12 | Ruin interaction and 6 s collection, rumors, recovery caches, the 10 s claim channel with interrupts, match phases, timer and results, a minimal economy | Same-tick claim and encounter ordering is deterministic (§5); a deadline claim is processed before the timeout | 2–3 |
| 6 | `slice-content` | §18 stage 2 | Four islands, two rubbing types, the Ember and Smoke kits (pedestals, 3 s eating) | §18 stage 2: explore, engage, steal, recover and claim in one 4-player match (a playtest) | 2 |

What slices 1 and 3 contain in detail:

- **Slice 1's duel simulation:** movement and guards, throw with a 10-frame escape window, the normal attacks and the Duelist's two specials, stamina, combo scaling with the 5-hit cap, and KO, draw and timeout. Hitstun and blockstun come from move data, and the state snapshots and restores for rollback.
- **Slice 3's netcode:** client prediction with checkpoint rollback and replay of unacknowledged inputs, a shared input delay of 3–8 frames, neutral input after 250 ms without a fresh one, reconnection, and a practice arena with a dummy.

**Capacity:** running 1 and 2 together is 3 lanes, and slice 3 on its own is 3. Both stay within the 3–4 lanes this VPS supports. Verification is the real bottleneck: one full test suite and one or two Playwright runs at a time.

**Why slice 1 is a single lane:** duel rules and move data are too tightly coupled to split. Lanes can't see each other's work until the candidate, so slice 3's three lanes need slice 1's duel API on `main` first. That makes slice 1 the "contract" slice for slice 3.

## Before the next launch
1. **Merge the skeleton into `main`**, so new features branch from it.
2. **Fix md-manager's `text_test_counts()` for Vitest**, or keep the reporter, which works.
3. **Update the launch line in `CLAUDE.md`** to drop `--reviewer-transport print`.

## Decisions I'd settle in each grill
- **Slice 1:** integer units for fighter physics and hitboxes (AABB in sub-pixels); the move-data schema (extending the §8 frame table already in `content`); only the Duelist kit.
- **Slice 3:** where the duel lives during the spike. I recommend a standalone practice or duel room hosting the same duel object that `MatchRoom` embeds in slice 4, per §14.

Two questions: should slice 1 (`duel-core`) come first, running in parallel with slice 2 (`world-sea`)? And should I set up those two features next (feature files, then a grill for each)?

import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

from .checks import text_test_counts
from .run_tests import counts


class RunTestsSummaryTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_child_summaries_are_counted_and_a_missing_summary_is_an_error(self):
        self.assertEqual(counts("...\nRan 3 tests in 0.1s\n\nOK (skipped=1)\n"), {"tests": 3, "failures": 0, "errors": 0, "skipped": 1})
        self.assertEqual(counts("Ran 4 tests in 1s\n\nFAILED (failures=1, errors=2)\n"), {"tests": 4, "failures": 1, "errors": 2, "skipped": 0})
        self.assertEqual(counts("Traceback: ImportError"), {"tests": 0, "failures": 0, "errors": 1, "skipped": 0})

    def test_parallel_summary_parses_like_a_plain_run_and_fails_when_a_class_fails(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
            package = Path(root) / "pkg"
            package.mkdir()
            (package / "__init__.py").write_text("")
            (package / "test_sample.py").write_text(
                "import unittest\n"
                "class A(unittest.TestCase):\n    def test_one(self): pass\n    def test_two(self): pass\n"
                "class B(unittest.TestCase):\n    def test_fails(self): self.fail('Ran 99 tests in 0s')\n"
                "    @unittest.skip('x')\n    def test_skipped(self): pass\n")
            result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "workflow.run_tests", "--jobs", "2", "pkg"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
                                    env={"PYTHONPATH": str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]), "PATH": ""})
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 1, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            # Child output is indented, so a child's own "Ran" line cannot be taken for the summary.
            self.assertEqual(text_test_counts(result.stdout), {"passed": 2, "failed": 1, "skipped": 1})
            self.assertIn("FAILED (failures=1, skipped=1)", result.stdout)
            (package / "test_sample.py").write_text("import unittest\nclass A(unittest.TestCase):\n    def test_one(self): pass\n")
            result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "workflow.run_tests", "pkg"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
                                    env={"PYTHONPATH": str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]), "PATH": ""})
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            self.assertEqual(text_test_counts(result.stdout), {"passed": 1, "failed": 0, "skipped": 0})


class RunTestsEchoTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_failed_classes_echo_their_whole_traceback_in_order_and_the_counts_still_parse(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
            package = Path(root) / "pkg"
            package.mkdir()
            (package / "__init__.py").write_text("")
            (package / "test_sample.py").write_text(
                "import subprocess, sys, unittest\n"
                "class Fails(unittest.TestCase):\n"
                "    def test_fails(self):\n"
                "        print('first, on stdout'); sys.stderr.write('second, on stderr\\n'); print('third, on stdout')\n"
                "        self.assertEqual(1, 2, 'the final failure line')\n"
                "    def test_passes(self): pass\n"
                "class Errors(unittest.TestCase):\n"
                "    def test_command(self):\n"
                "        subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', 'import sys; sys.stderr.write(\"fatal: the cause, on stderr\\\\n\"); sys.exit(128)'],\n"
                "                       check=True, capture_output=True)\n"
                "    def test_stray_bytes(self):\n"
                "        sys.stdout.buffer.write(b'\\xff not utf-8\\n'); sys.stdout.flush()\n"
                "        raise ValueError('the final error line, errors=7')\n")
            result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "workflow.run_tests", "--jobs", "2", "pkg"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
                                    env={"PYTHONPATH": str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]), "PATH": ""})
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 1, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            output = result.stdout
            # Every traceback reaches the log with its exception line; a failed command's stderr is noted under it.
            self.assertEqual(output.count("    Traceback (most recent call last):"), 3, output)
            self.assertIn("    AssertionError: 1 != 2 : the final failure line\n", output)
            self.assertRegex(output, r"\n    subprocess\.CalledProcessError: Command .* returned non-zero exit status 128\.\n(    .*\n)*?    fatal: the cause, on stderr\n")
            # Undecodable output neither stops the run nor hides the exception; child counts are respelled only.
            self.assertIn("\ufffd not utf-8\n", output)
            self.assertIn("    ValueError: the final error line, errors: 7\n", output)
            # stdout and stderr keep the order they were written in.
            self.assertIn("    first, on stdout\n    second, on stderr\n    third, on stdout\n", output)
            self.assertEqual(text_test_counts(output), {"passed": 1, "failed": 3, "skipped": 0})
            self.assertTrue(output.endswith("FAILED (failures=1, errors=2)\n"), output)

    def test_only_the_child_summary_line_counts(self):
        # A traceback or a noted command output quoting a summary is not the child's own result.
        output = ("E\nValueError: FAILED (errors=7)\nstderr of the failed command:\nRan 9 tests in 1s\n\nFAILED (failures=5)\n"
                  "----\nRan 2 tests in 0.1s\n\nFAILED (errors=1, skipped=1)\nsys:1: ResourceWarning: unclosed file\n")
        self.assertEqual(counts(output), {"tests": 2, "failures": 0, "errors": 1, "skipped": 1})

        self.assertEqual(counts("...\nRan 3 tests in 0.1s\n\nOK (skipped=1)\n"), {"tests": 3, "failures": 0, "errors": 0, "skipped": 1})
        self.assertEqual(counts("Ran 4 tests in 1s\n\nFAILED (failures=1, errors=2)\n"), {"tests": 4, "failures": 1, "errors": 2, "skipped": 0})
        self.assertEqual(counts("Traceback: ImportError"), {"tests": 0, "failures": 0, "errors": 1, "skipped": 0})

    def test_parallel_summary_parses_like_a_plain_run_and_fails_when_a_class_fails(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
            package = Path(root) / "pkg"
            package.mkdir()
            (package / "__init__.py").write_text("")
            (package / "test_sample.py").write_text(
                "import unittest\n"
                "class A(unittest.TestCase):\n    def test_one(self): pass\n    def test_two(self): pass\n"
                "class B(unittest.TestCase):\n    def test_fails(self): self.fail('Ran 99 tests in 0s')\n"
                "    @unittest.skip('x')\n    def test_skipped(self): pass\n")
            result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "workflow.run_tests", "--jobs", "2", "pkg"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
                                    env={"PYTHONPATH": str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]), "PATH": ""})
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 1, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            # Child output is indented, so a child's own "Ran" line cannot be taken for the summary.
            self.assertEqual(text_test_counts(result.stdout), {"passed": 2, "failed": 1, "skipped": 1})
            self.assertIn("FAILED (failures=1, skipped=1)", result.stdout)
            (package / "test_sample.py").write_text("import unittest\nclass A(unittest.TestCase):\n    def test_one(self): pass\n")
            result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "workflow.run_tests", "pkg"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
                                    env={"PYTHONPATH": str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]), "PATH": ""})
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            self.assertEqual(text_test_counts(result.stdout), {"passed": 1, "failed": 0, "skipped": 0})


class RunTestsEchoTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_failed_classes_echo_their_whole_traceback_in_order_and_the_counts_still_parse(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
            package = Path(root) / "pkg"
            package.mkdir()
            (package / "__init__.py").write_text("")
            (package / "test_sample.py").write_text(
                "import subprocess, sys, unittest\n"
                "class Fails(unittest.TestCase):\n"
                "    def test_fails(self):\n"
                "        print('first, on stdout'); sys.stderr.write('second, on stderr\\n'); print('third, on stdout')\n"
                "        self.assertEqual(1, 2, 'the final failure line')\n"
                "    def test_passes(self): pass\n"
                "class Errors(unittest.TestCase):\n"
                "    def test_command(self):\n"
                "        subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', 'import sys; sys.stderr.write(\"fatal: the cause, on stderr\\\\n\"); sys.exit(128)'],\n"
                "                       check=True, capture_output=True)\n"
                "    def test_stray_bytes(self):\n"
                "        sys.stdout.buffer.write(b'\\xff not utf-8\\n'); sys.stdout.flush()\n"
                "        raise ValueError('the final error line, errors=7')\n")
            result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "workflow.run_tests", "--jobs", "2", "pkg"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
                                    env={"PYTHONPATH": str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]), "PATH": ""})
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 1, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            output = result.stdout
            # Every traceback reaches the log with its exception line; a failed command's stderr is noted under it.
            self.assertEqual(output.count("    Traceback (most recent call last):"), 3, output)
            self.assertIn("    AssertionError: 1 != 2 : the final failure line\n", output)
            self.assertRegex(output, r"\n    subprocess\.CalledProcessError: Command .* returned non-zero exit status 128\.\n(    .*\n)*?    fatal: the cause, on stderr\n")
            # Undecodable output neither stops the run nor hides the exception; child counts are respelled only.
            self.assertIn("\ufffd not utf-8\n", output)
            self.assertIn("    ValueError: the final error line, errors: 7\n", output)
            # stdout and stderr keep the order they were written in.
            self.assertIn("    first, on stdout\n    second, on stderr\n    third, on stdout\n", output)
            self.assertEqual(text_test_counts(output), {"passed": 1, "failed": 3, "skipped": 0})
            self.assertTrue(output.endswith("FAILED (failures=1, errors=2)\n"), output)

    def test_only_the_child_summary_line_counts(self):
        # A traceback or a noted command output quoting a summary is not the child's own result.
        output = ("E\nValueError: FAILED (errors=7)\nstderr of the failed command:\nRan 9 tests in 1s\n\nFAILED (failures=5)\n"
                  "----\nRan 2 tests in 0.1s\n\nFAILED (errors=1, skipped=1)\nsys:1: ResourceWarning: unclosed file\n")
        self.assertEqual(counts(output), {"tests": 2, "failures": 0, "errors": 1, "skipped": 1})

def text_test_counts(log: str) -> dict | None:
    text = re.sub(r"\x1b\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]", "", log)
    unit = re.search(r"^Ran (\d+) tests? in .+$", text, re.MULTILINE)
    if unit:

        skipped = re.search(r"\bskipped=(\d+)", text)

        failures = sum(int(value) for value in re.findall(r"\b(?:failures|errors|unexpected successes)=(\d+)", text))
        if not re.search(r"^(?:OK(?:\s|$)|FAILED\s*\()", text, re.MULTILINE):

# Task: duel

## Goal

Build the deterministic 1v1 duel simulation of §7 and §8 as pure code: two fighters with the Duelist kit in one single-plane arena, stepped at 60 Hz from per-frame inputs, with snapshots that restore and replay exactly. This is the core that the combat spike (`duel-online`) will put online, and that the match room will later host as a duel object (§14). No rendering and no networking.

## Context

- Read `docs/spec.md` §7 (fighting system), §8 (controls and frame budgets), §15 ("Authoritative prediction policy": snapshots, restore, replay), §14 ("Match and duel boundaries") and §19 ("Combat determinism"). §9 describes the Duelist kit; §10's Haki abilities are deferred (see `decisions.md`).
- Read `docs/architecture.md` and the existing pure packages: `packages/simulation` (integer state, `hashState`, the seeded generator in `random.ts`, `fixed.ts`), `packages/content` (`frameBudgets.ts` already holds §8's baseline table with a zod validator) and `tests/unit/purity.test.ts`, which also scans any new directory under the pure packages.
- The verifier runs `npm ci`, then `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:integration` and `npm run build` (which ends with `scripts/smoke-build.ts`). It reads test counts from Vitest's summary; `tests/reporters/testSummary.ts` also prints them.
- Another feature (`world-sea`) runs at the same time on the rest of the repository. Stay inside your owned paths so the two merge cleanly.

## Constraints

- Owned paths only: `packages/simulation/src/duel`, `packages/content/src/moves`, `packages/test-tools/src/replay`, the three packages' `package.json` (only to add the subpath exports below) and `docs/duel.md`. Do not edit any existing source file, barrel `index.ts`, tsconfig, root file or `docs/architecture.md`.
- Expose the new code through subpath exports that follow the existing pattern (the `@pirate-sea-race/source` condition first, then `types` and `default` into `dist/`): `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/duel`, `@pirate-sea-race/content/moves`, `@pirate-sea-race/test-tools/replay`.
- Pure and integer, like the rest of `packages/simulation`: no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time, `Math.random` or floating-point transcendental `Math` functions. Every number in the duel state is a safe integer, so `hashState` covers it.
- The duel step is a function of (config, state, two inputs) that returns a new state and never mutates its input. Randomness, if any, comes from a seeded generator kept in the duel state.
- Out of scope: rendering, networking, rooms, protocol messages, fruit kits, Haki abilities, world integration, theft.

## Acceptance

- Duel rules from §7, covered by unit tests that drive the step with scripted input logs (one test per rule unless a rule is trivially shared):
  - one round, 60-second clock (3,600 frames), 1,000 health each; timeout → higher health wins; equal health → 10-second overtime, then compare, and an exact tie is a draw;
  - both simultaneous lethal hits → draw; a KO on the final round frame beats the timeout; both fighters' hits for a frame are evaluated before a KO is declared, independent of player order;
  - walk, crouch, jump, forward dash and backdash; fighters auto-face each other and stay inside the arena walls;
  - standing guard blocks highs and mids; crouching guard blocks lows, avoids highs and loses to mids; holding back guards and down-back guards low;
  - throws beat guard and have a 10-frame escape window; a throw escape is available to both players;
  - stamina: 100 max; dash costs 20; blocking a light costs 10, a heavy 25 and a special 20; regenerates 20 per second after one second without spending or blocking; a guard break staggers 30 frames and restores 30 stamina;
  - damage: jab 45, committed heavies and specials 100–150; combo scaling 100, 80, 65, 50 and 40 percent; the fifth damaging hit forces a non-juggleable recovery;
  - a 4-frame input buffer; both horizontal directions together are neutral (§8).
- Move data in `packages/content/src/moves`: the Duelist's normals (light/jab, heavy mid, low sweep, launcher, anti-air, throw) and its two specials (advancing thrust, counter slash), each with startup, active and recovery frames, integer hitboxes and hurtboxes, damage, hitstun, blockstun, guard level (high, mid, low, unguardable) and stamina cost. The jab, heavy mid, low sweep and throw match §8's baseline table. A zod validator rejects impossible data (non-positive startup or active frames, block advantage beyond active + recovery, hitboxes with no area, unknown move references), with unit tests.
- Frame advantage: a unit test shows the heavy mid is −12 on block, and that a jab started on the first frame the defender can act lands before the heavy's recovery ends (a punish).
- Determinism and rollback: the same initial state and input log give the same `hashState` after 3,600 frames; a one-input change gives a different hash; restoring a snapshot taken at frame N and replaying the logged inputs from N gives the same hash as the uninterrupted run.
- `packages/test-tools/src/replay`: a replay runner that loads an input log (a documented JSON format), runs it through the duel step and returns the final state and hash; it is used by at least the determinism tests.
- `docs/duel.md` (at most a page and a half): the state shape, the step's order of operations within a frame, the units, and how snapshot, restore and replay are meant to be used by the netcode.
- `npm ci` then `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:integration` and `npm run build` pass from a clean checkout, and the purity test covers the new directories.

## Stop

Report `blocked` instead of continuing when any of these happens:

- `npm ci` or an install fails twice for reasons outside the repository (registry, network).
- A rule in §7 or §8 contradicts another in a way that changes this acceptance.
- A check can pass only by changing a path outside the owned paths.
- After two hours of work, any required check still fails and you cannot name the next fix.

Report `question` only for a choice that would change this acceptance.

From the operator session of 2026-09-24 (slice planning after the skeleton merged into `main`). These are the recommended defaults; rerun `/workflow-grill duel-core` before launch to revise them.

## Decisions

- Scope is the pure duel simulation only (slice 1 of the plan). Networking, the arena client and the duel room are the next feature, `duel-online`, which builds against this feature's API from `main`. The API therefore has to be usable without changes: a step function, a snapshot that is plain data, and a replay runner.
- One lane (`duel`). Duel rules and move data are too coupled to split, and a split lane would fail its isolated typecheck against the other's types.
- Only the Duelist kit. Fruit kits (§9) come with the content slice; the Duelist's two specials are the advancing thrust and the counter slash.
- Haki abilities (§10: Armament, Observation parry, Resolve finisher) and the Haki meter are deferred. The spike's exit (§18: guard, punish, throw, simultaneous hit, reconnect) doesn't need them, and they add balance work before the core is proven.
- Units: integer sub-pixels, 16 sub-pixels per arena pixel. Positions, velocities, gravity and hitboxes are integers; hitboxes and hurtboxes are axis-aligned rectangles relative to the fighter's origin and facing.
- The code lives in new directories behind subpath exports (`@pirate-sea-race/simulation/duel`, `@pirate-sea-race/content/moves`, `@pirate-sea-race/test-tools/replay`), so this feature edits no existing file. `world-sea` runs at the same time on the rest of the repository, and the two branches must merge without conflicts.
- No browser check: nothing is rendered. The policy's checks are typecheck, unit, integration (unchanged, to prove nothing broke) and build (its smoke step proves the new subpath exports resolve from `dist/`).

- The arena is one plane with two walls and a floor; its width is content data. There's no stage hazard and no ring-out.
- A duel input per player per frame is a button bit field (light, heavy, special one, special two, dash) plus integer horizontal and vertical directions in {-1, 0, 1}, already as §8 maps keys. Keyboard mapping is client work.
- Frame data for moves outside §8's table (launcher, anti-air, the two specials) is the worker's choice within §7's ranges, documented in the move data.
- `hashState` from `packages/simulation` is reused for duel state, which also holds the duel's own frame counter and generator state if it needs one.
- The duel starts both fighters at fixed positions, facing each other, with full health and stamina, as §6 requires ("no free opening hit").

## Deferred

- Haki meter and abilities (§10), fruit kits (§9), focus scrolls.
- Networking, prediction and reconciliation, the input delay policy, reconnect: `duel-online`.
- Rendering, animation, the duel HUD and control remapping: `duel-online`.
- Hosting the duel inside `MatchRoom`, reservations, transitions and theft: `encounters-theft`.
